title: Prove It: Remainders and Checking
goal: I can divide with remainders, check my answer two ways, find mistakes, and decide what a remainder means in a story.

card.desc: Prove-it day before the winter break. Bailey solves mixed long division with remainders, uses a two-part check (the expression matches the dividend and the remainder is smaller than the divisor), finds and fixes mistakes in worked problems, and decides what remainders mean in stories. The break work is light and spread over two weeks, alongside the Holiday Gazette. Seven new words, including expression and retrace.

win: You accomplished long division with remainders. Enjoy a festive break!

slides.title: 817 ÷ 4: a zero and a remainder
slides.text: Say each step before you click. This one has a placeholder zero and a remainder.

steps.text: Divide. How many 4s fit in 8? 2 (4 × 2 = 8). Write 2 above the 8 in the hundreds place.
Multiply. 2 × 4 = 8. Write 8 under the 8.
Subtract. 8 − 8 = 0. Check: 0 is smaller than 4.
Bring down. Bring down the 1 from the tens place. The 0 and the 1 make 01, which is just 1.
Divide. How many 4s fit in 1? 0. Write 0 above the 1 in the tens place. Never skip the zero!
Multiply. 0 × 4 = 0. Write 0 under the 1.
Subtract. 1 − 0 = 1. Check: 1 is smaller than 4.
Bring down. Bring down the 7 from the ones place. Now you have 17.
Divide. How many 4s fit in 17? 4 (4 × 4 = 16; 4 × 5 = 20 is too big). Write 4 above the 7 in the ones place.
Multiply. 4 × 4 = 16. Write 16 under the 17.
Subtract. 17 − 16 = 1. Check: 1 is smaller than 4. There are no more digits to bring down, so 817 ÷ 4 = 204 R 1.

notes.do: She says each step and number BEFORE you click; she writes it on paper.
notes.say: Praise every correct step out loud: "Divide, 2. Yes!" "Zero, you were vigilant!" "R 1, and 1 is smaller than 4. Perfect."
notes.listen: The 0 in the tens place and the final remainder. If she skips the 0, ask: "Estimate first: about 20 or about 200?"

slides.title: Retrace your steps
slides.text: Fishlegs worked out 853 ÷ 6 and got 141 R 7. His check works: 141 × 6 + 7 = 853. So is he right?

steps.text: Look at the remainder: 7. The divisor is 6. 7 is not smaller than 6, so one more 6 fits.
Retrace the last step: 13 ÷ 6. 6 × 2 = 12 fits, so the digit is 2, not 1. 13 − 12 = 1.
Fixed: 853 ÷ 6 = 142 R 1. Check: 142 × 6 + 1 = 852 + 1 = 853 ✔ and 1 is smaller than 6 ✔

slides.tip: A good check has two parts: the expression matches the dividend AND the remainder is smaller than the divisor.

notes.do: Let her find the problem before you reveal Step 1. Give her a full minute.
notes.say: When she finds it: "Diligent! The check alone did not catch it, but you did."
notes.ask: "Why did the multiplication check still work?" (141 × 6 + 7 is the same total; it just has an extra 6 hiding in the remainder.)
notes.listen: She checks BOTH parts: the expression and the remainder rule.

items.q: Snotlout worked out 817 ÷ 4 and got 24 R 1. Check: 24 × 4 + 1 = 97, not 817. Find the mistake in the work.
choices: Nothing is wrong. The answer is accurate.
A placeholder 0 is missing in the quotient. The answer is 204 R 1.
items.why: A placeholder 0 is missing in the quotient. The answer is 204 R 1. Fix it and finish: 817 ÷ 4 = 204 R 1. Check: 204 × 4 + 1 = 817.
no: 3 × 4 = 12. That is too big.
Check: 24 × 4 + 1 = 97, not 817. That discrepancy means there is a mistake.
Check it: that subtraction is correct.

slides.title: The check is an expression
slides.text: Write the check as one expression: quotient × divisor + remainder. Multiply first, then add.
slides.tip: Multiply before you add. 154 × 6 + 1 is not 154 × 7.

slides.title: The whole routine
slides.text: Tap the steps in the order a seasoned mathematician uses them for a story problem.
steps: Read the story and write the division.
Check: the expression matches and the remainder is smaller than the divisor.
Read the question again and decide what to do with the remainder.
Write the answer with a label.
slides.why: Read, estimate, solve, check, decide, label.
slides.hint: You check your long division before you decide what the remainder means.

notes.do: She says all six from memory before tapping.
notes.listen: Estimate before solving; check before deciding.

sets.q: Hiccup has 90 cents. A fish costs 8 cents. How many fish can he buy? What do you do with the remainder?
choices: Drop the remainder: use only the quotient
Round up: add 1 to the quotient
sets.why: Only full groups count, so the leftovers are dropped.
no: Read the question again: does it ask how many are left over?
Read the question again: does it ask about everything fitting, or only full groups?

sets.q: Having lots of practice and experience is being ____. (Use a word from your word cards.)
sets.why: Seasoned means having lots of practice and experience.
sets.no: It starts with sea-.

sets.q: To accomplish a goal means to…
sets.why: To accomplish is to finish something successfully.
no: Forgetting is the opposite.
Starting over is not finishing.
Retrace means go back over steps.

practice.intro: Three tries on each one, but only your first try counts. Keep paper and a pencil next to you. Solve, check both parts, and let the context decide.

questions.q: Use long division: 86 ÷ 5 = ____   (use R for the remainder)
questions.no: Go one step at a time. At the end, whatever is left after the last subtraction is the remainder.

questions.q: Use long division: 938 ÷ 7 = ____   (use R for the remainder)
questions.no: Go one step at a time. At the end, whatever is left after the last subtraction is the remainder.

questions.q: Use long division: 509 ÷ 4 = ____   (use R for the remainder)
questions.no: Go one step at a time. At the end, whatever is left after the last subtraction is the remainder.

questions.why: 127 × 4 = 508, and 508 + 1 = 509. It matches the dividend, so the answer is right.
questions.no: Multiply 127 × 4 first. Then add the remainder 1.

questions.q: Fishlegs worked out 775 ÷ 6 and got 128 R 7. Check: 128 × 6 + 7 = 775. The check matches, but the answer is still wrong. Why?
choices: A placeholder 0 is missing in the quotient.
He forgot to bring down a digit.
Nothing is wrong. The check matches.
The remainder 7 is not smaller than 6, so the last digit of the quotient is too small. It should be 9.
questions.why: The remainder 7 is not smaller than 6, so the last digit of the quotient is too small. It should be 9. Fix it and finish: 775 ÷ 6 = 129 R 1. Check: 129 × 6 + 1 = 775.
no: Every place in the quotient has a digit.
Every digit was brought down.
The check matches, but a remainder of 7 breaks the rule: it must be smaller than 6.

questions.q: 170 Vikings sail. Each longship holds 8. How many longships are needed?
questions.why: 170 ÷ 8 = 21 R 2. 21 is not enough: 2 would be left out. Round up: 22 longships.
questions.no: Divide first: 170 ÷ 8. Then read the question again: what does it ask for?
questions.hint: Can the leftover ones be left behind? If not, you need one more.

questions.q: Gobber has 83 nails. A bag holds 9. How many bags can he fill?
questions.why: 83 ÷ 9 = 9 R 2. Only 9 are full; the 2 left over cannot make another one. Drop the remainder: 9 bags.
questions.no: Divide first: 83 ÷ 9. Then read the question again: what does it ask for?
questions.hint: Can the leftover make a full one? If not, do not count it.

questions.q: 142 fish are shared equally among 6 dragons. How many fish are left over?
questions.why: 142 ÷ 6 = 23 R 4. The question asks what is left over, so the answer is the remainder: 4 fish.
questions.no: Divide first: 142 ÷ 6. Then read the question again: what does it ask for?
questions.hint: The question asks how many are LEFT. Which part of the answer is that?

questions.q: Numbers and operation signs written together make an ____. (Use a word from your word cards.)
questions.why: An expression is numbers and signs written together.

questions.q: Cheerful and full of celebration is ____. (Use a word from your word cards.)
questions.why: Festive means cheerful and full of celebration.

questions.q: Which shows how to keep your momentum over the break?
choices: Stop all practice for two weeks.
Do a little math and reading each week.
questions.why: Momentum keeps you moving forward. A little practice each week keeps it going.
no: Stopping loses momentum.
Forgetting loses momentum.
That does not keep your skills moving.

teacher.objective: Bailey proves Week 7 before the break: mixed long division with remainders (2- and 3-digit dividends, placeholder zeros, first digit too small), a two-part check (the expression quotient × divisor + remainder matches the dividend AND the remainder is smaller than the divisor), finding and fixing mistakes in worked problems, and deciding what a remainder means in a story (round up, drop it, or the remainder is the answer).
materials: Class lesson on your laptop or tablet (teacher code 9110)
Paper and a pencil for Bailey
3 sticky notes: Round up, Drop it, Remainder is the answer
Her book, How to Train Your Dragon
Packet (2 pages): done in the second week of the break

plan.do: Class slide 1. Ask about Tuesday's check and the Lesson 16 packet.
Class slide 2. Most important event this week, how Hiccup and Toothless changed (two events), a prediction; how far she will read over the break.
Class slide 3. 53 Vikings in boats of 6 (round up to 9); check 79 ÷ 6.
Class slide 4. Her own sentence for each word; expression and retrace on the whiteboard.
Class slides 5–6. She says each step before you click (placeholder 0 and R 1); then 94 ÷ 4, 925 ÷ 6, 437 ÷ 7 on paper. Praise every correct step.
Class slides 7–8. Fishlegs's 141 R 7 (check matches, remainder too big); Snotlout's missing zero; Hiccup's subtraction slip.
Class slides 9–10. Multiply first, then add; check 437 ÷ 7; revise a remainder of 9 for ÷ 9.
Class slide 11. 40 beans in cups of 6 for the tables story; then barrels and coins.
Class slide 12. Six steps in order from memory.
Class slide 13. Diligent, retrace, expression; momentum and festive in her own sentences.
Class slide 14. 719 ÷ 3, check 653 ÷ 4, egg cartons; note any miss for January.
Class slide 15. Course page: Lesson 18 break list, the two Long Division Lane links, and the Holiday Gazette card.

watch: Trusting a check that matches when the remainder is too big (141 R 7 for ÷ 6). Ask: "Part 2 of the check: is the remainder smaller than the divisor?"
Adding before multiplying in the check (154 × (6 + 1)). Say: "Multiply first, then add the remainder."
Omitting a placeholder zero when there is also a remainder (817 ÷ 4 = 24 R 1). Ask for an estimate: about 20 or about 200?
Dropping the 0 at the end of a quotient (165 ÷ 8 = 2 R 5 instead of 20 R 5). Ask: "Did you bring down every digit? What did you write after the last one?"
Giving "8 R 5 boats" in a story. Ask: "Is that practical? Read the question again."
"I can't do it" before the break, when she is tired. Ask only for the first step, praise it out loud, then the next.

packet_key.answer: expression → numbers and signs written together; retrace → to go back over the same steps; diligent → working hard and carefully; accomplish → to finish successfully; festive → cheerful and full of celebration; momentum → energy that keeps you moving forward; seasoned → having lots of practice
The remainder 11 is not smaller than 6, so one more 6 fits: 83 ÷ 6 = 13 R 5 (13 × 6 + 5 = 83).
100 ÷ 7 = 14 R 2 → the remainder: Stoick keeps 2 coins
Answers vary; uses accomplish correctly with a real example problem.
Answers vary; describes a change with an event from the book and uses seasoned or diligent correctly.
